Biochemical and microbial changes reveal how aerobic pre-treatment
impacts anaerobic biodegradability of food waste
Henry Fisgativa, Anne Tremier ⇑, Mohamed Saoudi, Sophie Le Roux, Patrick Dabert
Irstea, UR OPAALE, 17 avenue de Cucillé, CS 64427, F-35044 Rennes Cedex, France

Food waste
a b s t r a c t
Aerobic pre-treatment of food waste (FW) was performed at different oxygen concentrations (0%, 5%, 10%
and 21%O2) and different durations (1, 2, 3 and 4 days) to investigate its impact on biochemical and
microbial community characteristics of the waste and its ability to improve anaerobic biodegradability.
Whatever the duration, the highest effect of pre-treatment was observed at full aerobic pre-treatment
(21%O2) while 5%O2 and 10%O2 showed lower transformation performances. Biochemical variations at
21%O2 were mainly a decrease of simple carbohydrates, volatile fatty acids (VFA) and low molecular
weight water soluble compounds and an increase of high weight water soluble compounds. Microbial
community analysis showed a clear modiﬁcation of populations after 21%O2 aerobic pre-treatment,
changing from an initial dominance of lactic acid bacteria to a ﬁnal dominance of VFA consumers
(like Acetobacter) and a higher presence of Fungi. Enzymatic tests showed an increase of exoenzymes
content and a higher presence of protein and carbohydrates degrading enzymes. Finally, the aerobic
pre-treatment did not negatively impact methane potential of FW (496 NLCH4kgVS1) which remained
unchanged after two days of pre-treatment at 21%O2. These latter optimal pre-treatment conditions are
proposed to be tested in future investigation of anaerobic digestion (AD) process with low inoculum to
substrate ratio in order to assess their ability to avoid acidiﬁcation risk during AD of FW.

1. Introduction
The management and treatment of food waste (FW) is a subject
of growing interest worldwide. In Europe, about 89 Mt of FW are
produced each year, mainly by households and food services
(53% and 12% of the total FW respectively) (Monier et al., 2010;
Stenmarck et al., 2016). Beyond waste prevention, EU is thus pro-
moting FW valorisation, essentially via composting or anaerobic
digestion (article 5 of EU Directive 99/31/EC).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has proven to be an appropriate tech-
nique to treat FW, resulting in the production of an energy-rich
biogas and a digestate which can be used as biological fertiliser
(Li et al., 2011; Zamanzadeh et al., 2016). However, the stability
and efﬁciency of AD of FW can be problematic on two points. On
short-term, a rapid accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFA),
caused by the high concentration of simple carbohydrates in FW,
may inhibit methane production (Ren et al., 2018; Scano et al.,
2014; Zhang et al., 2012). A total inhibition can be observed at a
VFA concentration of 40–50 gCODL1 (Veeken and Hamelers,
2000). On longer term, anaerobic conditions result in slow hydrol-
ysis kinetics and only partial degradation of the structural carbohy-
drates of FW: only about 50% of the cellulose is degraded after
30 days of AD (Deublein and Steinhauser, 2011). Moreover, fer-
mentation during storage step between the collection of the FW
and its introduction in the AD treatment can produce an additional
VFA accumulation contributing to instability (Fisgativa, 2016).
Several studies have been conducted to improve the AD yield
and stability, using mechanical, thermal, chemical or enzymatic
pre-treatments of the substrates (Brémond et al., 2018; Carrere
et al., 2016; Kondusamy and Kalamdhad, 2014). Even though some
pre-treatments demonstrated their ability to enhance AD, side
effects as the release of recalcitrant and inhibitory molecules or
further difﬁculty for digestate dewatering were also observed.
These undesired phenomena, in addition to the difﬁculty of imple-
mentation and high energy requirements of pre-treatments, often
counteracted their positive effects (Carlsson et al., 2012; Ma
et al., 2011). In comparison, the interest of a biological aerobic
pre-treatment of substrates before AD has been revealed more
recently with a real potential. Indeed, it has been shown that
pre-treating FW enhances the hydrolysis of slowly biodegradable
compounds by promoting the microbial excretion of hydrolytic
enzymes (Charles et al., 2009; Lim and Wang, 2013; Meng et al.,
2016; Sarkar and Venkata Mohan, 2017). Ni et al. (2017) stated

was also observed by Raﬁeenia et al. (2017) on methane produc-
tion with one day pre-aerated (5 Lh1) protein-rich FW. However,
the duration and conditions of aerobic pre-treatment should be
well managed to not oxidise excessively the organic matter of
FW and limiting the methane yield. Brummeler and Koster
(1990) observed that 10-days of aerobic pre-treatment, on the
organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW), resulted in
lower initial acid formation during AD linked to the degradation
of the easily degradable part of the substrate but induced a loss
of 40% of methane production. Wu et al. (2018) showed that an
aerobic storage of FW during 8 days produced a diminution of
15% of the methane yield comparing to raw FW. Charles et al.
(2009) showed that carbon emitted as CO2 (during six days of pres-
suring aerobic pre-treatment of OFMSW), accounts for the reduc-
tion of 26% of the CH4 produced during subsequent AD. Finally,
Raﬁeenia et al. (2017) observed that even a short (one day) aerobic
pre-treatment causes a decrease of methane potential of a lipid-
rich FW, compared to a non-pre-aerated sample.
In spite of these studies, there is still a lack of knowledge on the
biochemical and microbial community modiﬁcations promoted by
such aerobic pre-treatments while there is a real challenge at the
industrial level in assessing the ability of aerobic pre-treatment
to limit the risk of instabilities potentially occurring during AD of
FW. The aim of this study was thus (1) to understand how short

biodegradability of the waste and which variations of FW charac-
teristics (physicochemical characteristics, biochemical fractiona-
tion, microbial populations and enzymes content), promoted by
the pre-aeration explain this inﬂuence; and (2) to highlight which
pre-treatment condition could be interestingly later tested in AD
process conditions. The impacts of the oxygen level and of the
pre-treatment duration were speciﬁcally assessed. Compared to
previously published experiments that were performed at small
laboratory scale (1-L bottles) with grounded FW (Meng et al.,
2016; Raﬁeenia et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018), our study was rea-
lised at a 10-L laboratory pilot scale with raw FW.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Composition and sampling of food waste feedstock
The study used FW (kitchen waste and leftovers of the dishes
served) produced by a collective catering establishment, which
produces 17 tons of waste per year, corresponding to nearly 700
customers per day. FW was collected over a period of three days
(stored at 4 C) and mixed to obtain a representative sample with
the following typological composition: 30% vegetables, 24% fruits,
19% meat, 13% starchy food, 9% bones and shells and 5% paper
per wet weight (WW). Initial FW (hereafter referred to as T0 or
raw FW) was sub-sampled and stored at 20 C for later use in
the experiments to ensure the same initial feedstock conditions.
The characteristics of the raw FW (analysed as described in Sec-
tions 2.4 and 2.5 below) are listed in Table 1.
2.2. Experimental pre-treatment set-up
The pre-treatment pilot consisted of four 10-L glass cells
equipped with a gas ﬂow inlet and outlet. The cells containing
3 kg of FW were maintained in a water bath heated by an auto-
mated thermostat at a temperature of 37 C. This temperature is
close to conditions of mesophilic AD processes. The temperature
within the cell contents was recorded using a Platinum resistance
thermometer. The pre-treatment tests were carried out by circulat-
ing 50 Lh1 of gas, to optimise the aerobic degradation of FW as
described by Tremier et al. (2005), with a recirculation rate of
300 Lh1 to ensure homogeneous conditions. The inlet of gas
was located at the bottom of the cell and the gas ﬂowed through
the waste to reach the outlet located at the top of cell. The O2 con-
tent in the gas ﬂow entering the experimental cell was set at 0%,
5%, 10% or 21% by mixing compressed air with nitrogen (N2) to
study the effects of anaerobic conditions (0%O2), limited oxygen
conditions (5%O2 and 10%O2) and ambient air or full aeration con-
ditions (21%O2). Incoming and outgoing O2, CO2, N2O and CH4 con-
centrations in the air of each cell were measured at 3-min intervals
using an ABB gas analyser (model URAS26EL3020, ABB).
Because it is not possible to get a homogeneous FW sample
from a cell without disturbing waste characteristics, doing a time
course experiment required running as many cells as the number
of samples needed. Thus, for each O2 concentration, four cells were
started at the same time and one cell was stopped every day of the
4-day experiment in order to collect and sample the waste and to
measure variations in FW characteristics. Along this paper, the
durations of 1, 2, 3 and 4 days of pre-treatment, regardless the oxy-
gen conditions, will be also referred as T1, T2, T3 and T4 respec-
tively. The maximal duration of 4 days of pre-treatment was
chosen to limit excessive organic matter degradation in aerobic
conditions according to previous studies (Charles et al., 2009).
The total content of each cell, thereafter called treated FW, was
immediately homogenised and frozen at 20 C prior to analyses.
2.3. Samples preparation
One kilogram of each frozen sample (raw FW and treated FW
from each cell) was ground to 2 mm using a Robot Coupe R15 Food
Processor for physicochemical and biochemical analyses. About 7 g
of these ground FW samples were further ground in liquid nitrogen
for 1 min with a ball mill (300 Dangoumill, Prolabo) to obtain a
homogeneous powder, which was stored at 80 C for further
molecular microbiology and enzymatic analyses.
2.4. Physicochemical and biochemical analyses
Total solids (TS) were analysed after drying at 80 C until con-
stant weight. Volatile solids (VS), chemical oxygen demand (COD)
total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN) and ammonium (NH4

sured using standard methods (APHA, 2012).

2.5. Anaerobic biodegradability tests
To determine the methane yield of raw and treated FW, the bio-
logical methane potential (BMP) tests were performed according to
NF EN ISO 11734 standard as described by Vedrenne et al. (2008).
Measurements were made in triplicate using hermetically closed
572 ml-bottles, containing 40 ml of inoculum and 3–5 g of ground
FW (raw or treated) (ratio 1 gVS inoculum:1 gVS FW as recom-
mended by Parra-Orobio et al. (2018) and Hobbs et al. (2018)).
Measurements were performed on raw FW (T0) and at 2 and 4 days
of pre-treatment for each oxygen condition. Samples from 1 and
3 days pre-treatment were not analysed because of limitation on
experimental schedule. The inoculum was obtained from a well-
established anaerobic pilot digester (87 L) acclimated to degrade
pig slurry supplemented with horse feed. The bottles were incu-
bated at 38 C for about 40 days. Daily pressure measurements
enabled quantiﬁcation of biogas production. Biogas was then sam-
pled for CH4 and CO2 analysis by gas chromatography equipped
with an electron capture detector (Agilent Technologies, 6890N,
USA) according to the method described by Lucas et al. (2007).
2.6. Characterisation and dynamics of FW microbial community
The microbial community of each sample was analysed as
described in detail by Fisgativa et al. (2017). Brieﬂy, total DNA
was extracted from about 200 mg of frozen ground FW using the
Macherey Nagel Genomic DNA for Food kit. Bacterial and fungal
communities of samples were quantiﬁed by SSU rRNA-targeted
real-time qPCR using generic primers. Bacterial and archaeal diver-
sity was determined by high throughput DNA sequencing of the
16S rRNA gene V4-V5 variable regions using Ion TorrentTM PGM
technology (Life Technologies, USA) at the IRSTEA BIOMIC team
(Antony, France) (Poirier et al. (2016). Between 20,796 and
83,525 DNA sequences were obtained per sample that were pro-
cessed and clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs,
based on 97% similarity) using the QIIME software. Taxonomic
identiﬁcation of the OTUs was done on the Ribosomal Database
Project database (https://rdp.cme.msu.edu/). OTUs containing less
than 1% of the total number of sequences of all samples were con-
sidered as subdominant. Fungal diversity was investigated by col-
lecting mycelium on day 4 of the 21%O2 pre-treatment condition,
extracting DNA and cloning and sequencing of a 422 bp fragment
of the 18S rRNA genes. The sequences were aligned against the
NCBI database for identiﬁcation using Blast software (NCBI,
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST).
2.7. Determination of enzymes
2.7.1. Total hydrolytic exoenzymes activity
The extracellular enzymes (exoenzymes) present in the sample
hydrolyse the ﬂuorescein diacetate (FDA) into ﬂuorescein, a soluble
molecule which can be quantiﬁed by ﬂuorescence (Emission 530).
The method used in this study was adapted from Adam and
Duncan (2001). The reagents used (potassium phosphate buffer
(60 mM, pH 7.6); (b) FDA stock solution (stored at 20 C); and
(c) Pure ﬂuorescein (Sigma-Aldrich Co. Ltd) stock solution (stored
at 4 C in the dark)) were prepared as described by Adam and
Duncan (2001).
For the analyses, 5 g of frozen ground FW were mixed with
50 ml sterile water and vigorously stirred with a stomacher (Sto-
macher 400, Tekmar, Cincinnati, OH, USA) for 10 min. After
10 min of decantation, centrifugation was performed at 3000g at
4 C for 10 min. Next, 2 ml of supernatant were mixed with
15 ml of potassium phosphate buffer solution and 0.2 ml of FDA
solution in a 40 ml ﬂask. The ﬂask was closed, mixed by hand
and placed on an orbital incubator (150 rpm) at 37 C for 30 min.
Control samples were prepared without the addition of FDA. After
incubation, 15 ml of acetone were added immediately to stop the
reaction. After 10 min of decantation, the content of each ﬂask
was centrifuged (3000g at 4 C for 3 min). The supernatant was ﬁl-
tered (Whatman, No.2) and analysed in a black microwell plate
with a ﬂuorimeter (GloMax-Multi Detection System, Promega).
Pure ﬂuorescein diluted with potassium phosphate buffer (0–
6 mgml1) was used as calibration solution, showing the following
relation:

2.7.2. Hydrolytic exoenzyme activities
The enzymatic activities present in the water extracts were
determined using an APIZYM kit (BioMérieux Co, France) according
to the supplier’s instructions. The kit allows rapid monitoring of 19
hydrolytic enzymatic activities (proteases, glucosidases, lipases,
etc.) without the need for puriﬁcation. 65 ll of ﬁltered supernatant
used for the FDA analysis were placed in each well. The APIZYM
gallery was covered and incubated at 37 C for 4 h. After incuba-
tion, one drop of reagent ZYM A (BioMérieux Co, France) and one
drop of reagent ZYM B (BioMérieux Co, France) were added to each

2.8. Statistical analyses
One factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to iden-
tify a difference between pre-treatment trials. In the cases that
ANOVA tests were signiﬁcant with p-value < 0.05, Fishers Least
Signiﬁcant Difference (LSD) tests were used to further investigate
between groups.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Impact of O2 concentration and pre-treatment duration on further
anaerobic biodegradability
3.1.1. Biodegradation kinetics of FW during aerobic pre-treatment
During the 1–4 days of aerobic pre-treatment, variations in the
kinetics of gas production (CO2, CH4 and N2O) were monitored on
line to analyse aerobic and anaerobic metabolic activities. No pro-
duction of CH4 or N2O was observed whatever the O2 concentration
in the entering gas ﬂow, showing that methanogenesis or partial
nitriﬁcation/denitriﬁcation activity did not take place during the
pre-treatment (data not shown). Concerning CO2, a ﬁrst peak of
production was observed in all conditions during the ﬁrst day of
pre-treatment (Fig. 1a) This CO2 emission can result from biological
activities such as respiration or fermentation, but also from physic-
ochemical phenomena such as modiﬁcation of the calco-carbonic
balance. The fact that a similar amount of CO2 was emitted during
the ﬁrst day without strong difference in the temperature increase
(Fig. 1c), and whatever the O2 level of the pre-treatment, suggests
an abiotic process. This is conﬁrmed by the CO2:O2 ratio (Fig. 1b)
which was higher at 5% and 10%O2 pre-treatments than at 21%O2
during the ﬁrst day, revealing the absence of a relation between
O2 consumption and CO2 production, and which is also in accor-
dance with the presence of that peak in anaerobic conditions (with-
out O2 consumption). Thus, the CO2 peak observed during the ﬁrst
day of pre-treatment does not appear to be linked with the
biodegradation process but rather with the degassing of carbonates
present in FW. It results from the punctual disequilibrium induced
between the gaseous phase and the solid aqueous phase by the
establishment of the gas ﬂow within the waste medium.
After one day of pre-treatment however, visible differences
appeared between the different pre-treatment conditions. With
0%O2, a minimum but constant production of CO2 (2.5 mmol CO2-
kgTS1h1) was observed probably corresponding to microbial
fermentation. In the low and fully aerobic conditions, CO2 produc-
tion rose, revealing a constant relation with O2 consumption
(Fig. 1a and b) and conﬁrming an aerobic biological activity. These
results are in agreement with those obtained by Botheju et al.
(2010), who reported an increase in CO2 generation with increasing
O2 load during an aerobic pre-treatment between 0% and 10%O2
aeration on primary wastewater sludge. Moreover, our data
(Fig. 1a) show that the production of CO2 at 5%O2 and 10%O2 pre-
treatment is similar but low compared to the one at 21%O2. The
total production of CO2 at 4 days (T4) was 2255, 2435 and
4091 mmolCO2kgTS1 at 5%, 10% and 21%O2 experiences respec-
tively. These data show twice stronger biological activity, and thus
biodegradation, at 21%O2 compared to 5%O2 and 10%O2 pre-
treatments. This observation is in line with the proposal of Haug
(1993) stating that, for composting, O2 concentrations lower than
10% in the air result in lower organic matter decomposition. Inter-
estingly, even with experimental cells maintained in a ther-
mostated bath, the increased biodegradation linked to biological
respiration led to heat release and temperature increase (Fig. 1c),
traducing the large extent of the aerobic exothermic reactions.
Considering this high aerobic activity, organic matter degradation
was quantiﬁed and BMP analyses were performed to assess the
ability of these pre-treated FW to produce biogas in AD.

On longer pre-treatment duration, analyses showed signiﬁcant

Given the different kinetics of biological activity observed dur-

treated FW.
3.1.3. Anaerobic biodegradability of the pre-treated FW
Table 2 shows that methane yield measured based on wet
weight, decreases with time during the pre-treatments. The differ-
ence was not statistically signiﬁcant between the raw FW (T0) and
the two-day pre-treated waste. However, a signiﬁcant decrease (p-
value = 0.01) of almost 7% was observed after 4 days of pre-
treatment for all pre-treatment conditions (with the exception of
10%O2). This reduction is consistent to the overall decrease on VS
and COD assessed after 4 days of pre-treatment. These results con-
ﬁrm that an extended pre-treatment of FW is deleterious for fur-
ther use of the waste in AD as also observed by Xu et al. (2014a).
Looking at the methane yield expressed on a VS basis, it appears
that BMP also decreased by 6.5% with 4 days of a 0%O2 pre-
treatment (p-value = 0.04). It means that the most biodegradable
organic matter was degraded during the pre-treatment leading to
a less biodegradable residual organic matter for AD.
Interestingly, this reduction of the organic matter biodegrad-
ability was not observed for 4-day pre-treated FW with 5%O2,
10%O2 and 21%O2 conditions, as their BMP expressed on a VS basis
was not signiﬁcantly different from the one of raw FW. These
results suggest that the VS consumed by micro-organisms and
mineralised into CO2 during the aerobic pre-treatment, was bal-
anced by changes in the quality of the residual VS content.
This hypothesis is reinforced when looking at the cumulative
methane production curves. During the 10 ﬁrst days of the BMP
test, methane production is higher with pre-treated waste at 21%
O2 (378 NLCH4kgVS1) (p-value = 0.01) than with raw FW (328
NLCH4kgVS1) (Fig. 2c). With 5%O2 pre-treated waste, methane
production kinetics is comparable (after two days (T2) (314
NLCH4kgVS1) (p-value = 0.11)) or slightly lower (after four days
(T4) (285 NLCH4kgVS1) (p-value = 0.01)) than with raw FW (T0)
(328 NLCH4kgVS1) (Fig. 2a). It can thus be assumed that the
organic fractions of FW which were recalcitrant to anaerobic
degradation when considering raw FW became more available
and easily biodegradable thanks to the aerobic pre-treatment,
especially with oxygen conditions higher than 10%.
To conﬁrm this hypothesis and understand in depth the effect of
the aerobic pre-treatment on the quality of the FW organic matter,
its variations of composition, the biomass development and enzy-
matic activities were further studied.
3.2. Relation between variations in the biochemical characteristics of
FW during aerobic pre-treatment and further anaerobic
biodegradability
3.2.1. Variations in biochemical fractionation
To understand the variations in the quality of the FW organic
matter during aerobic pre-treatment, a modiﬁed Van Soest frac-
tionation was performed on all samples. This method allows dis-
cretising the total organic matter into several compartments of
different putative biodegradability.

3.2.2. Variations in simple carbohydrates and VFA concentrations
To investigate variations in the water soluble organic fractions
(SOLW > 1.5 kDa and SOLW < 1.5 kDa) more in detail, their concen-
trations in simple carbohydrates (sucrose, glucose and fructose)
and VFA were monitored. Fig. 4 shows that the simple carbohy-
drates content decreased regularly with time in both aerobic and
anaerobic conditions. The unexpected strong decrease occurring
on the third day of the 0% condition may be due to an undesired
inﬁltration of air for about 12 h before stopping the cell. Aside from
this uncontrolled result, the decrease in simple carbohydrates con-
tent was seen to be ampliﬁed by higher O2 pre-treatment (Fig. 4a). It
resulted in 80% removal of the total simple carbohydrates from the
raw FW at high oxygenation (21%O2, T4). In comparison, only 26% of
the total simple carbohydrates were degraded in anaerobic condi-
tions (0%O2, T4). This simple carbohydrates diminution can be
related to the diminution of the SOLW < 1.5 kDa fraction (Fig. 3)
and the high CO2 production (Fig. 1a) at high O2 concentration.
The VFA content was monitored in parallel showing an increase
in their concentration with time in anaerobic conditions and lim-
ited oxygen condition (0% and 5%O2), conﬁrming microbial fermen-
tations (Fig. 4b). In aerobic conditions, the accumulation of VFA
was lower, with a slight decrease after 4 days at 10%O2 (30% less
than at 0%O2 T4) and a marked decrease at 21%O2 T4 (60% lower
than 0%O2 T4), which is clearly linked to the increase of pH from
5.3 to 6.2 at the latter condition as observed on Table 2. These
results are consistent with previous reports of Raﬁeenia et al.
(2017), using aeration pre-treatment in a two phase anaerobic
digestion of FW, which observed a positive effect of pre-aeration
on the reduction of VFA accumulation during the second stage of
AD. The observed diminution in accumulation of VFA may result,
either from the reduced availability of simple carbohydrates pro-
ducing VFA as can be seen in Fig. 4a, or from a rate of VFA con-
sumption higher than that of their production during high O2
concentration pre-treatment.
Biochemical characteristics studied in this section give a better
understanding of the BMP variations observed after aerobic pre-
treatment. The stability of BMP can be attributed mainly to a pos-
itive effect of aerobic pre-treatment that produces a shift in the
biodegradable molecules distribution: a diminution of very easily
biodegradable molecules (SOLW < 1.5 kDa fraction, simple carbohy-
drates), and an increase of the supply of soluble water molecules
(SOLW > 1.5 kDa fraction), recovered from the non-soluble frac-
tions. These changes might help in case of subsequent AD, avoiding
rapid simple carbohydrates consumption and therefore rapid VFA
accumulation, making more rapidly available the less biodegrad-
able molecules and conserving methane yield.

4. Conclusion
In this work, four O2 concentrations (0%, 5%, 10% and 21%) were
tested as pre-treatment of FW with 4 different durations (1, 2, 3
and 4 days). The results suggested that aerobic pre-treatment of
FW could be used before anaerobic digestion to improve waste
biodegradability and also to limit the detrimental effect of acidiﬁ-
cation. Pre-treatments with limited oxygen (5% and 10%O2) are less
efﬁcient and also more difﬁcult to implement. Prolonging pre-
treatment at 21%O2 up to 4 days reduces signiﬁcantly the FW
methane potential, so the cost-beneﬁt of its implementation needs
to be evaluated on a case by case basis. A short aerobic pre-
treatment (up to 4 days) strongly modiﬁes the microbial commu-
nity of FW promoting the presence of fungi and VFA consuming
bacteria like Acetobacter which may contribute to limit VFA accu-
mulation. It enhances the solubilisation of the waste organic mat-
ter and thus allows a preservation of the waste methane potential.
To conclude, since VFA accumulation may lead to real instabilities
and operational difﬁculties during FW anaerobic digestion, a short
aerobic pre-treatment appears as an interesting and robust option
to be tested to facilitate FW AD management, especially consider-
ing dry processes with low inoculum to substrate ratio.
